extracted.intended_audience: CRTC Commissioners, regulatory staff, and applicants (broadcasting and telecommunications licensees)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and recommended procedural standards for handling interrogatories, tariff filings, hearing panels, decision-making, and the drafting of decisions in CRTC broadcasting and telecommunications proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commission as control centre for interrogatories
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission should act as a control centre for interrogatories to avoid duplication and irrelevance; it should gather and vet all questions desired to be asked by interveners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical benefits include use of a single consecutive numbering scheme to identify interrogatories; the Commission should take the initiative early to gather and vet the questions, decide which must be answered, publish a list, and obtain the responses. This process is recommended both for original and supplementary interrogatories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standardized interrogatories and numbering
rubrics_metrics.description: Standardize interrogatories for rate hearings and use a single consecutive numbering scheme to identify them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standardization reduces repetition and cross-referencing confusion. A single numbering system helps keep materials organized when many interveners submit questions and answers that otherwise create confusion and duplicate work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interrogatory pre-conference and service procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Interveners prepare a complete list of proposed interrogatories after filing evidence and serve the list on all parties including the Commission; a conference chaired by a senior official is held to address relevance, duplication, confidentiality, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommended procedural steps: (a) each intervener who wishes to submit interrogatories prepares a complete list after evidence filing; (b) the list is served on all parties and the Commission; (c) a chaired conference is held for representations on relevance/duplication/confidentiality; (d) the Commission decides which questions must be answered and publishes the list; (e) same procedure for supplementary interrogatories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tariff filing supporting documentation requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Tariff filing guidelines should spell out kinds of supporting information required for various categories of tariff revisions; for new or competitive services an economic evaluation must accompany the filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Economic evaluations should show that the service has been priced so as not to be a burden on other services. The Commission prepared 'Tariff Filing Guidelines' to specify supporting information required. Staff-level analysis by tariff specialists should screen filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Streamlined processing for routine tariff applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Routine tariff matters should be processed primarily at the staff level and, if acceptable, sent to two Commissioners for approval rather than convening a full Tariff Committee meeting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delegation to staff specialists saves senior staff and Commissioners' time; two experienced Commissioners could sign necessary orders following consultation with the Director of Tariffs. This preserves committee time for significant items and avoids convening large committees for routine matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness expectation for tariff application decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: For the majority of tariff applications, decisions should be announced promptly (noted target: within 30 days of filing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While new procedures initially caused delay, most wrinkles can be ironed out and routine applications can be decided quickly if processes are streamlined and handled at staff level with limited commissioner involvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard hearing panel composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Except for matters of special significance, the standard hearing panel should consist of not more than three members: two full-time and one part-time member from the region affected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A three-member panel (majority full-time) balances regional input with continuity and helps control local bias. Larger panels reserved only for matters the Commission deems of significant importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Part-time members' voting rights on matters they hear
rubrics_metrics.description: Part-time members should have the right to vote on the applications they hear, changing their role from consultant to adjudicator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Granting part-time members vote equality for items they heard promotes natural justice, makes hearing participation meaningful, and encourages a more objective and 'judicial' approach. Legislative changes may be required, but organizational changes can give practical effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hearing panels should make and sign final decisions promptly
rubrics_metrics.description: The panel of three members that heard an application should make, write and sign on behalf of the Commission final decisions on their hearing items as soon as possible after the hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Giving panels final decision-making power avoids multi-stage processes that cause delay, reduces reliance on Commissioners who did not hear the matter, improves fairness to parties, and strengthens compliance with natural justice. Panels writing decisions increases accountability and depth of reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-hearing preparation for panel members
rubrics_metrics.description: Panel members, including part-time members, should be involved earlier: receive original files when notices are published (50 days in advance), be given issue sheets, and be advised of likely applications requiring appearances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attach an 'issue sheet' prepared by staff highlighting key issues and relevant policies to each file; circulate additional materials and internal memoranda as they become available. Early preparation reduces need for extensive staff briefings and allows panels to plan lead questioners and lines of questioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elimination of consultation stage for specific licensing applications
rubrics_metrics.description: If the panel that heard an application also decides it, the consultation stage with other Commissioners (who did not sit at the hearing) should be eliminated for specific licensing applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consultation normally delays decisions and often involves Commissioners who have not thoroughly reviewed files; meaningful information is already available through published notices, decisions, information circulars, and brief presentations. Removing consultation speeds decisions and avoids token participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Telecommunications decisions rule: panel decides after sworn evidence hearings
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions following public telecommunications hearings in which witnesses are sworn and cross-examined should, as a general rule, be taken by the panel of Commissioners assigned to deal with them; collegial decision-making remains for other proceedings (policy hearings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because credibility, demeanour, and hearing of evidence matter, panels that heard sworn testimony are better placed to decide. Collegial discussion may still occur for policy issues separate from the merits of particular applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commissioners who heard matters should draft decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Where possible, the Commissioners who heard applications should write the decisions rather than relying primarily on staff drafting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Staff-drafted decisions often lack fully spelled-out reasons and risk staff acting as de facto decision-makers. Having hearing Commissioners draft decisions forces them to consider facts and arguments closely, improves the quality of reasoning, and ensures that all relevant factors were weighed. Drafts may then be circulated for comment and the Chairman signs the final decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checks against regional/local bias in part-time members
rubrics_metrics.description: To guard against a part-time member's judgment being overly swayed by local or regional concerns, ensure panels have a full-time majority and reframe part-time roles toward adjudication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A majority of full-time members on a three-member panel and changing the role of part-time members to 'adjudicator' both promote objectivity and a judicial approach to decision-making while still preserving regional insight.
